subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 11 periods = 495 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 8h 15min

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
periods.activity_title: The Compass That Moves: Detecting Current's Magnetic Effect
periods.activity_description: A magnetic compass is placed under a current-carrying wire connected in a simple circuit with a switch. Students observe the compass needle's deflection when the switch is closed and its return when the switch is opened, recording both states.

roles.role_description: Sets up the circuit demonstration, guides students to observe the compass needle position before and after closing the switch, and draws attention to the disappearance of deflection when current stops.
Take turns closing and opening the switch, observe and sketch the compass needle position in both states, and record their observations in a table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter's opening story of the lifting electromagnet at the science exhibition and poses the central question: does electric current have a magnetic effect?
Groups set up the compass-under-wire circuit, take turns closing and opening the switch, and record needle positions in both states in a structured observation table.
Each group shares their recorded observations; class compares results and notes that needle deflection is consistent and reversible with current flow.
Teacher introduces the term 'magnetic field' and consolidates the key concept: a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that disappears when current stops.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's entry point, so orient students to the two big phenomena — magnetic and heating effects — before narrowing to today's focus on the compass experiment. A common error is that students think the compass deflects because the wire itself is a magnet rather than because current flows through it; press them to predict what happens when the switch is opened to surface this. A quick checkpoint: students are ready to move on when they can state that deflection depends on current flowing, not on the wire alone.

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
periods.activity_title: Nail, Wire, and Clips: Building the First Electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students wind insulated wire around an iron nail, connect it to a cell, and test how many iron paper clips the nail attracts when current flows and when current is off. They record both states and notice that clips fall when current stops.

roles.role_description: Wind wire around the nail, close the circuit to attract clips, count the clips held, then open the circuit and observe the clips falling, recording all observations.
Circulates to ensure safe winding technique and asks probing questions about why the clips fall when the switch opens.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's finding that current produces a magnetic field, then poses a new question: can we use this effect to make a magnet that we can switch on and off?
Groups wind wire around the iron nail, connect the circuit, test clip attraction with current on and off, and record the number of clips held in each state.
Groups share their counts and observations; class discusses why clips are held only when current flows and what role the nail plays.
Teacher introduces the term 'electromagnet' and its defining characteristic: a current-carrying coil that behaves as a magnet only while current flows.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the previous unit's compass finding, students now see the magnetic effect put to use in a controllable device. Watch for groups who wind the wire in alternating directions, which weakens the effect; guide them to wind consistently in one direction. A useful probe is to ask why a permanent magnet could not do the same job as the electromagnet in a lifting crane.

periods.activity_title: Coil, Core, and Compasses: Mapping the Poles of an Electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students form a cylindrical coil on a paper cylinder, place compasses at both ends, and insert an iron nail into the core. They observe which end of the coil behaves as the North pole and which as the South pole, comparing their electromagnet's pole structure to a bar magnet.

roles.role_description: Construct the coil on the paper cylinder, position compasses at each end, pass current, observe compass deflections, and identify which end is North and which is South.
Guides groups to interpret compass deflection direction as indicating pole type, and asks students to draw the analogy between their coil and a bar magnet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's definition of an electromagnet and poses the question: does an electromagnet have poles like a bar magnet?
Groups construct the paper-cylinder coil, connect to a cell, place compasses at both ends, and observe the direction each compass needle points to identify the poles.
Groups insert the iron nail into the coil's core and observe whether the number of clips attracted (or compass deflection) changes compared to the air-core coil.
Class discussion: students classify the electromagnet as having a North pole and a South pole, and discuss why the iron core increases its strength.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit moves from simply observing that a coil attracts to classifying the electromagnet's properties by comparing it to a bar magnet — a deliberate step up in cognitive demand from the previous two units. Students often assume that both ends of the coil are alike; the compass readings at each end should challenge this directly. Confirm that groups can name which end is North and which is South before moving on.

periods.activity_title: More Cells, More Turns: Investigating What Controls Electromagnet Strength
periods.activity_description: Students systematically vary the number of cells (one versus two) and the number of wire turns around the nail, recording how many paper clips are held in each condition. They also reverse the current and observe what happens to the poles.

roles.role_description: Carry out the controlled investigation by changing one variable at a time — number of cells, then number of turns — recording clip counts, and finally reversing the battery to observe pole reversal.
Emphasises keeping all other variables constant while one is changed, and asks groups to predict the outcome before each trial.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's pole-classification findings and introduces the investigation question: what factors control how strong the electromagnet is?
Groups test one cell versus two cells (holding turns constant) and record the number of clips held in each condition.
Groups vary the number of turns (holding cells constant) and record results, then reverse the battery connections and observe the compass response at each end of the coil.
Class compiles results and draws conclusions: strength increases with more current and more turns; poles reverse when current direction is reversed.

periods.teacher_notes: Coming from the previous unit's pole-identification work, students are now ready to investigate the variables that control electromagnet behaviour — a richer classification task. A common procedural error is changing both cells and turns at the same time; model the concept of changing one variable while holding others constant before groups begin. Students ready to progress should be able to state two factors that increase strength and explain what reversing the battery does to the poles.

periods.stage_label: Explain the mechanism and application of the magnetic effect
periods.activity_title: From Coil to Crane: How Lifting Electromagnets Work
periods.activity_description: Students examine how the electromagnet properties they have investigated — switchable magnetism, pole structure, and variable strength — are applied in industrial lifting electromagnets mounted on cranes. They construct a written explanation of how a crane operator uses current to hold and release heavy metal objects.

roles.role_description: Presents the lifting electromagnet application through description and questioning, connecting each design feature back to what students observed in their own electromagnet investigations.
Write a short explanation of how a lifting electromagnet works, citing the properties — switchable field, iron core, current magnitude — that make it suited for the task.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects this unit to the previous two units by reminding students of the three properties they established: switchable field, pole structure, and strength control.
Teacher describes lifting electromagnets on cranes and how the operator controls the circuit to hold and release scrap metal, linking each feature to students' own experimental findings.
Students individually write a causal explanation: why an electromagnet is more suitable than a permanent magnet for this industrial task, using the properties they know.
A few students share their explanations; class refines the causal reasoning together, focusing on the role of switchable current.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units built the empirical base; this unit asks students to use it causally — explaining why the electromagnet's properties make it the right tool for a crane application. Students frequently say the crane 'uses electricity to be magnetic' without connecting this to the switchable nature of the field; push them to explain what the operator does with the switch and why a permanent magnet would not work. The written explanation is the checkpoint: it should mention current, iron core, and switchability.
materials: Blackboard or display surface for description

periods.stage_label: Explain the mechanism and application of the magnetic effect
periods.activity_title: Wire Gets Warm: Observing the Heating Effect of Current
periods.activity_description: A nichrome wire is connected in a circuit. Students touch the wire before and after current flows, and record their observations. They then use two cells instead of one and compare the warmth produced, establishing that greater current produces more heat.

roles.role_description: Touch the nichrome wire before closing the switch, then after current has flowed, and record the temperature change felt; repeat with two cells and compare.
Manages safety during the touch test, ensures students note the difference between one-cell and two-cell conditions, and introduces the term 'heating effect of electric current'.

time_bands.activity: Teacher transitions from the magnetic effect strand to the second major phenomenon: does a current-carrying wire get hot? Students predict the answer before any experiment.
Groups connect the nichrome wire circuit, touch the wire before switching on, close the switch briefly, and carefully touch again, recording the change in warmth.
Groups repeat with two cells and compare the warmth felt to the one-cell condition, recording observations and noting the trend.
Teacher introduces the term 'heating effect of electric current' and the concept of resistance, explaining that the conductor resists current flow and converts electrical energy to heat.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's second major strand; remind students that the magnetic and heating effects both arise from current flowing through a conductor, linking the two strands at the outset. The most common misconception is that only 'special' wires heat up; the nichrome wire is chosen because its high resistance makes the effect obvious, but all conductors convert some energy to heat. Safety note: keep the switch closed only briefly to avoid excessive heating of the nichrome wire.

periods.stage_label: Explain the mechanism and application of the magnetic effect
periods.activity_title: Useful and Wasteful Heat: Connecting the Heating Effect to Appliances
periods.activity_description: Students examine a list of electrical appliances — room heaters, irons, kettles, and hair dryers — and identify in each what the heating element is and what its function is. They then sort the same effect into 'useful' and 'problematic' categories using examples from the chapter.

roles.role_description: Examine the appliance list, identify the heating element and its function in each device, and then sort heating-effect examples into useful and problematic categories with written justifications.
Facilitates discovery by asking groups to explain why the heating element is a rod or coil of wire rather than a flat plate, and introduces the industrial electric furnace example.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's finding that resistance converts electrical energy to heat, then asks: where do we see this deliberately used in everyday life?
Groups examine the appliance list, identify what serves as the heating element in each device, and write one sentence on what function the heat serves.
Groups sort heating-effect instances into useful applications and problematic consequences — energy loss, overheating, melting, fire risk — with a brief justification for each placement.
Class discussion consolidates the dual nature of the heating effect: intentionally exploited in appliances and furnaces, but an energy loss and safety risk in transmission and uninsulated wiring.

periods.teacher_notes: Coming from the hands-on observation of the previous unit, this unit asks students to classify and explain the heating effect across contexts — a move from observation to causal reasoning about applications. Students often treat 'heating effect' as purely positive; deliberately prompt them to name at least two problematic consequences from the chapter before ending the sorting task. Groups that can articulate why the heating effect is both useful and problematic are ready to move on.
materials: Printed or written list of appliances and their descriptions

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain how cells and batteries supply current
periods.activity_title: Lemon Power: Constructing a Voltaic Cell
periods.activity_description: Students build a Voltaic cell using a lemon, a copper wire, and an iron nail as electrodes, connecting them to a LED. They observe the LED lighting up and identify which materials act as electrodes and which as the electrolyte, connecting this to the structure of a Voltaic cell.

roles.role_description: Insert copper wire and iron nail into a lemon, connect them to a LED, observe whether the LED lights, and record which electrode is positive and which is negative.
Introduces the Voltaic cell's structure — two different metal electrodes in a liquid electrolyte — before the activity, and guides students to map each part of their lemon cell onto this structure.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the new strand: where does the current in a circuit come from? Students are told about the Voltaic cell's basic structure — two different metal electrodes in a liquid electrolyte — with the historical Galvani-Volta story as context.
Groups construct the lemon Voltaic cell, connect it to a LED, and observe whether the LED lights; they then label which electrode is positive (copper) and which is negative (iron nail).

Groups record the mapping: lemon juice as electrolyte, copper wire as one electrode, iron nail as the other, and discuss what drives the current — a chemical reaction between the electrodes and the electrolyte.
Teacher consolidates the concept of the Voltaic cell: chemical energy is converted to electrical energy; the cell 'dies' when the chemicals are used up.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the chapter's third strand and shifts from effects of current to sources of current — make this transition explicit so students see it as part of one larger story. A frequent confusion is that students think the lemon itself is the power source; redirect them to the role of the lemon juice as an electrolyte enabling a chemical reaction between two different metals. Groups are ready to move on when they can identify the three components — two electrodes of different materials and an electrolyte — in their own lemon cell.

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain how cells and batteries supply current
periods.activity_title: Inside the Dry Cell: Structure, Function, and Limits
periods.activity_description: Students examine the structural components of a dry cell — zinc container, carbon rod, metal cap, and paste electrolyte — and explain the function of each component. They compare the dry cell to the Voltaic cell and identify what makes the dry cell more practical.

roles.role_description: Describes the internal structure of the dry cell with a labelled diagram and questions students on how each structural component maps onto the Voltaic cell's principles.
Complete a labelled diagram of the dry cell and write the function of each component, then list two ways the dry cell improves on the Voltaic cell.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's Voltaic cell structure and asks students what limitations a liquid-electrolyte cell would have in everyday use.
Teacher presents the dry cell's internal structure with a labelled diagram; students annotate their own diagram identifying zinc container, carbon rod, metal cap, and paste electrolyte.
Students individually write the function of each structural component and list two ways the dry cell is more practical than the Voltaic cell (portable, no liquid spillage).
Class discussion addresses the dry cell's limitation: it is single-use and must be disposed of safely because it contains acids and toxic metals.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the lemon-cell activity of the previous unit, students are now ready to see how the same principles — two different materials and an electrolyte — are engineered into the compact dry cell. Students often confuse the carbon rod with the positive terminal itself; clarify that the carbon rod sits inside and the metal cap on top is the positive terminal the circuit connects to. The disposal safety point about acids and toxic metals is worth pausing on, as it connects to the chapter's own safety sidebar.
materials: Blackboard diagram or printed diagram of dry cell cross-section

periods.stage_label: Construct and explain how cells and batteries supply current
periods.activity_title: Single-Use to Rechargeable: Comparing Types of Cells
periods.activity_description: Students compare single-use dry cells and rechargeable batteries across several criteria — energy source, reusability, applications, and end-of-life concerns — and arrange them in a structured comparison table, then evaluate which type is more appropriate for a given set of uses.

roles.role_description: Construct a comparison table for single-use dry cells and rechargeable batteries across the four criteria, then evaluate which type suits a list of given applications and justify each choice.
Circulates and prompts groups to consider the environmental and resource-scarcity concerns around lithium-ion batteries mentioned in the chapter.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the previous unit's dry cell structure and limitation, then poses the question: are there cells that can be recharged and reused, and how do they differ from single-use cells?

Groups construct a four-criterion comparison table for single-use and rechargeable cells using information from the chapter: energy source, reusability, typical applications, and end-of-life concerns.
Groups evaluate a short list of applications — wristwatch, electric vehicle, phone, TV remote — and decide which cell type is most appropriate for each, writing a brief justification.
Class shares evaluations; teacher introduces the Li-ion battery and solid-state battery details, and reinforces the chapter's safe disposal message for all cell types.

periods.teacher_notes: Coming from the previous unit's structural understanding of the dry cell, this unit asks students to evaluate rather than just describe — a move up in cognitive demand. Students often assume rechargeable cells are straightforwardly better in every situation; the resource-scarcity concerns around lithium and cobalt, and the limited number of charge cycles, are worth raising as genuine trade-offs from the chapter. Groups ready to advance should be able to name a situation where a single-use cell might still be preferred and justify it.
materials: Printed or written list of applications for the evaluation task

periods.stage_label: Reason across magnetic effect, heating effect, and cell operation to explain circuit behaviour
periods.activity_title: One Circuit, Three Questions: Connecting Magnetic Effect, Heating Effect, and Cell Operation
periods.activity_description: Students are given a scenario circuit — a cell, a switch, a nichrome heating element, and a coil wrapped around an iron nail — and must reason through what happens magnetically, thermally, and at the cell level when the switch is closed. They produce a written analysis linking all three effects.

roles.role_description: Analyse the scenario circuit and produce a written response answering three linked questions: what magnetic effect occurs and why, what heating effect occurs and why, and what is happening inside the cell that drives both effects.

Introduces the scenario, clarifies that all three chapter strands must appear in a complete answer, and facilitates a class discussion that surfaces and corrects any remaining disconnects between the three phenomena.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the integrated scenario circuit and explains that a complete answer to the three questions requires connecting everything covered across this chapter's units.
Students individually analyse the circuit and write responses to all three questions — magnetic effect, heating effect, and cell operation — connecting the phenomena with causal language.
Students share responses in pairs, identify any gaps or contradictions, and refine their explanations; teacher listens for persistent misconceptions to address in the whole-class discussion.

Whole-class consolidation: teacher draws out the thread connecting all three — the cell drives current, the current produces a magnetic field in the coil and heat in the nichrome wire simultaneously, demonstrating that electricity's effects are concurrent, not sequential.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit asks students to reason across all three chapter strands simultaneously, which is the highest cognitive demand of this plan. Students often treat the magnetic and heating effects as separate topics rather than concurrent phenomena in the same circuit; the scenario circuit is designed to make both visible at once. A strong individual response will name the cell as the source, explain resistance as the mechanism for heat, and connect current direction to the electromagnet's pole structure — all three in one causal chain.
materials: Diagram of the scenario circuit (drawn on blackboard or printed)
homework: Sketch a simple circuit that would both ring an electric bell (using an electromagnet) and warm a wire at the same time, and explain in two or three sentences which component produces each effect and why.

A dry cell in a TV remote stops working after a month, while a rechargeable battery in a phone lasts two years. Explain this difference using the concepts of chemical reaction, electrolyte, and recharging from this chapter.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe compass needle deflection caused by current flow and construct a basic electromagnet with a nail, recording how clip attraction switches on and off with the circuit.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can describe, from direct observation, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that is present only while current flows, and that winding current-carrying wire around an iron nail creates a switchable magnet.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students identify the North and South poles of their electromagnet using compasses, then systematically vary current magnitude and number of turns to classify the factors that control strength and observe that reversing current reverses the poles.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can identify the North and South poles of an electromagnet, classify the variables that increase its strength (current magnitude, number of turns), and demonstrate that reversing the current direction reverses the poles.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain the mechanism and application of the magnetic effect
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students explain how electromagnet properties are used in lifting cranes, observe and measure the heating effect of current in a nichrome wire, and classify heating-effect instances as useful applications or problematic consequences.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can explain why an electromagnet's switchable field makes it suitable for lifting cranes, and can explain that resistance converts electrical energy to heat, classifying the heating effect as both a useful tool in appliances and a source of energy loss and hazard.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Construct and explain how cells and batteries supply current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a lemon Voltaic cell, map the structure of a dry cell onto the same principles, and evaluate single-use versus rechargeable batteries across criteria of reusability, application, and environmental concern.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can identify the components of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain that a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces electrical current, and evaluate which cell type is more appropriate for a given application with justification.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Reason across magnetic effect, heating effect, and cell operation to explain circuit behaviour
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse a scenario circuit containing a heating element and an electromagnet powered by a cell, and produce a written explanation that causally links cell operation, current flow, magnetic field production, and heat generation simultaneously.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: The student can produce a causal explanation of how a cell drives current that simultaneously produces a magnetic field in an electromagnet coil and heat in a resistance element, integrating cell chemistry, the magnetic effect, and the heating effect in a single coherent account.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can describe, from direct observation, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that is present only while current flows, and that winding current-carrying wire around an iron nail creates a switchable magnet.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works and demonstrate its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A magnetic compass is placed under a wire connected to a battery and a switch. When the switch is closed, the compass needle deflects. When the switch is opened again, what happens to the compass needle, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: The needle deflects further because opening the switch causes a surge of current.

options.label: B
options.text: The needle points toward the battery because the battery is the source of the magnetic field.

options.label: C
options.text: The needle returns to its original position because the magnetic field disappears when current stops flowing.

options.label: D
options.text: The needle stays deflected because the wire retains magnetism after the current stops.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Indicates the misconception that the wire itself becomes permanently magnetised by the current — the student has not grasped that the magnetic field is produced by the current, not stored in the wire.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Indicates a confusion between switching a circuit off and creating an electrical surge — the student lacks understanding of what happens to current flow when a switch opens.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Indicates the misconception that the battery is the locus of the magnetic field rather than the current-carrying wire — the student has not connected conductor position to field production.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with verbal reasoning about causes may be asked first to mime or draw the needle position in each switch state before selecting an option. Students who answer quickly can be asked to predict what would happen if the wire were replaced with a plastic rod carrying no current.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can describe, from direct observation, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that is present only while current flows, and that winding current-carrying wire around an iron nail creates a switchable magnet.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works and demonstrate its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Condition | Switch State | Number of clips held by nail
1 | Open | 0
2 | Closed | 7
3 | Open | 0
4 | Closed | 7
assessment_items.question_text: A wire is wound around an iron nail and connected to a cell with a switch. Refer to the table provided. Which conclusion is best supported by the pattern in the table?

options.label: A
options.text: Closing the switch changes the nail's material from iron to a magnetic alloy.

options.label: B
options.text: The clips are attracted to the cell, not to the nail, when the switch is closed.

options.label: C
options.text: The iron nail is a permanent magnet that is activated by the switch.

options.label: D
options.text: The nail attracts clips only when current flows through the coil, showing the magnetic effect is produced by the current.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals the misconception that the electromagnet behaves like a permanent magnet — the student has not registered the repeating on-off pattern in the data.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a misattribution of the magnetic effect to the cell rather than to the current-carrying coil around the nail.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misconception that the switching action causes a physical material change in the nail rather than a temporary magnetic effect from current.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find table reading difficult may first describe in words what they notice happening each time the switch state changes before selecting an answer. Students who find the pattern immediately can be asked what they would predict for a fifth row with the switch closed.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the North and South poles of an electromagnet, classify the variables that increase its strength (current magnitude, number of turns), and demonstrate that reversing the current direction reverses the poles.

competency.competency_text: Investigate and describe properties of natural and artificial magnets, including Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student winds 20 turns of insulated wire around an iron nail and connects it to one cell. A compass placed at End X of the coil shows its North pole pointing toward End X. The student then reverses the battery connections. What will the compass at End X show after the reversal?

options.label: A
options.text: The compass needle will point away from the nail because the iron core stops being magnetic when current changes direction.

options.label: B
options.text: The compass will show its South pole pointing toward End X because reversing current direction reverses the electromagnet's poles.

options.label: C
options.text: The compass will show no change because reversing the battery does not affect the electromagnet's poles.

options.label: D
options.text: The compass will spin continuously because the electromagnet loses all directionality when the battery is reversed.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals failure to connect current direction to pole identity — the student treats the electromagnet's poles as fixed properties like those of a permanent magnet.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a misconception that reversing the battery creates an unstable or undefined magnetic state, rather than a definite reversed polarity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals confusion between stopping current entirely (which does eliminate the field) and reversing current (which reverses the field) — the student merges two distinct experimental conditions.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the scenario may first draw the original compass position and the reversed battery arrangement before predicting the outcome. Students who answer quickly can be asked what would happen to the compass at the opposite end of the coil at the same moment.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the North and South poles of an electromagnet, classify the variables that increase its strength (current magnitude, number of turns), and demonstrate that reversing the current direction reverses the poles.

competency.competency_text: Investigate and describe properties of natural and artificial magnets, including Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Trial | Number of cells | Number of turns | Clips held
1 | 1 | 20 | 5
2 | 2 | 20 | 9
3 | 1 | 40 | 9
4 | 2 | 40 | ?
assessment_items.question_text: A student investigates what controls the strength of an electromagnet. Refer to the table provided. Based on the pattern in the data, which prediction for Trial 4 is most reasonable, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: About 13 or more clips, because both more current and more turns increase strength, so their combined effect should exceed either alone.

options.label: B
options.text: About 2 clips, because using more cells depletes the battery faster and reduces the magnetic force.

options.label: C
options.text: About 5 clips, because doubling both cells and turns cancels out the effects.

options.label: D
options.text: About 9 clips, because the number of turns has already reached its maximum effect in Trial 3.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a failure to read the directional trend in the data — the student has not identified that both variables independently increase strength.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a misconception that the effect of number of turns reaches a ceiling after one doubling — the student has not applied the trend logically to a combined condition.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals the misconception that battery depletion during an experiment reduces current mid-trial, a confusion between long-term battery drain and instantaneous current magnitude.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the table may first describe in words what changes between Trials 1 and 2 and between Trials 1 and 3 separately before being asked to reason about Trial 4. Students who answer quickly can be challenged to sketch what a fifth trial with 3 cells and 40 turns might show.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the North and South poles of an electromagnet, classify the variables that increase its strength (current magnitude, number of turns), and demonstrate that reversing the current direction reverses the poles.

competency.competency_text: Investigate and describe properties of natural and artificial magnets, including Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student builds an electromagnet using 30 turns of wire around an iron nail connected to one cell. She wants to make the electromagnet stronger and also needs to reverse which end is the North pole. Describe two changes she should make to achieve both goals, and explain why each change produces its intended effect.
expected_elements: Identifies increasing the number of turns or adding a second cell (increasing current) as a way to increase strength.
Explains why the chosen change increases strength — more turns means more wire contributing to the field; more cells means more current, and greater current produces a stronger magnetic field.
Identifies reversing the battery (or current direction) as the way to reverse which end is the North pole.
Explains that reversing current direction reverses the direction of the magnetic field in the coil, and therefore which end becomes North and which becomes South.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write may list their two changes as bullet points with a single explanatory phrase rather than full sentences. Students who complete the task quickly may be asked to describe what the compass at each end of the coil would show before and after the reversal.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the mechanism and application of the magnetic effect
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain why an electromagnet's switchable field makes it suitable for lifting cranes, and can explain that resistance converts electrical energy to heat, classifying the heating effect as both a useful tool in appliances and a source of energy loss and hazard.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works and demonstrate its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A crane in a scrap yard uses an electromagnet to pick up and move metal objects. A worker needs to release a heavy piece of metal precisely into a collection bin. Which action achieves this, and why is a permanent magnet not used for this job?

options.label: A
options.text: The worker insulates the electromagnet; insulation blocks the magnetic field and allows release, while a permanent magnet cannot be insulated.

options.label: B
options.text: The worker opens the circuit switch; the magnetic field disappears instantly because it depends on current, while a permanent magnet cannot be switched off.

options.label: C
options.text: The worker reduces the number of wire turns; fewer turns weaken the magnet enough to drop the load, while a permanent magnet has too many poles.

options.label: D
options.text: The worker reverses the battery; this pushes the metal off the magnet, while a permanent magnet would do the same if reversed.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals confusion between pole reversal (which would re-attract the object from a different pole, not release it) and switching off the field — the student has conflated two distinct control mechanisms.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals partial understanding — the student knows turns affect strength but treats a reduction in turns as a viable real-time control mechanism, not recognising that the switch is the practical control.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals the misconception that magnetic fields can be blocked by electrical insulation, confusing insulation of electrical current with blocking of magnetic fields.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the two-part question challenging may answer each part separately — first: how to release the metal; second: why not use a permanent magnet. Students who respond quickly may be asked what would happen if the crane's power supply failed mid-lift.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain the mechanism and application of the magnetic effect
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain why an electromagnet's switchable field makes it suitable for lifting cranes, and can explain that resistance converts electrical energy to heat, classifying the heating effect as both a useful tool in appliances and a source of energy loss and hazard.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works and demonstrate its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student connects a nichrome wire in a circuit. After current flows, she notices the wire becomes warm. She then connects two cells instead of one and finds the wire becomes much hotter. Which explanation correctly accounts for both observations?

options.label: A
options.text: Nichrome wire heats up because it is made of a special heat-generating material that reacts with air; more cells push more air through the wire.

options.label: B
options.text: The heating is caused by friction between electrons and the nichrome wire, but the amount of heat stays constant regardless of how many cells are used.

options.label: C
options.text: The resistance of the nichrome wire converts electrical energy to heat; more cells provide greater current, which produces more heat in the same resistance.

options.label: D
options.text: The wire heats up because the battery itself generates heat and conducts it through the wire; more cells mean more heat from the battery.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misconception that the heating is a chemical reaction between the wire and air rather than a conversion of electrical energy due to resistance — a common alternative conception about wire heating.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals misattribution of heat generation to the battery rather than to the conductor's resistance — the student has not connected resistance in the wire to the energy conversion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals partial understanding — the student has grasped a mechanism (resistance/friction) but has not connected greater current to greater heat production, treating the heating as constant.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the two-observation structure may be asked to explain one observation at a time before combining them. Students who respond quickly may be asked what would happen to the heating if a copper wire of the same length replaced the nichrome wire, given that copper has lower resistance.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can explain why an electromagnet's switchable field makes it suitable for lifting cranes, and can explain that resistance converts electrical energy to heat, classifying the heating effect as both a useful tool in appliances and a source of energy loss and hazard.

assessment_items.question_text: An electric iron and a long-distance power transmission line both carry electric current, and both get hot. Explain why heating is useful in one case and a problem in the other, using the concept of resistance and energy conversion in your answer.
expected_elements: States that resistance in the iron's heating element converts electrical energy to heat, and this heat is the intended output — it is what presses and smooths cloth.
States that resistance in transmission line wires also converts electrical energy to heat, but this heat is wasted energy that was meant to reach homes and factories.
Uses the concept of resistance as the mechanism for heat production in both cases.
Distinguishes the two cases by whether the heat is the desired output or an unwanted loss.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to write a connected explanation may draw two labelled boxes — one for the iron and one for the power line — and write one sentence in each about what happens to the heat. Students who complete quickly may be asked to name two other appliances that deliberately exploit the heating effect and one other context in which the heating effect is a problem.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain how cells and batteries supply current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the components of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain that a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces electrical current, and evaluate which cell type is more appropriate for a given application with justification.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works and demonstrate its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student inserts a copper wire and an iron nail into a lemon and connects them to a LED, which lights up. Which statement correctly identifies what acts as the electrolyte and explains why current flows?

options.label: A
options.text: The copper wire is the electrolyte; it allows electrons to flow from the iron nail to the LED.

options.label: B
options.text: The iron nail is the electrolyte; its rust reacts with the copper to produce electricity.

options.label: C
options.text: The LED itself generates the current when light strikes it; the lemon merely keeps the wires in place.

options.label: D
options.text: The lemon juice is the electrolyte; a chemical reaction between the two different metals and the lemon juice drives a current through the circuit.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals confusion between the role of a conductor (wire) and an electrolyte — the student has not grasped that the electrolyte is a liquid medium for a chemical reaction, not a current-carrying wire.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a detail confusion within the activity — the student has misidentified the nail (electrode) as the electrolyte, possibly because rust is a chemical change that is visible on the nail.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a fundamental misattribution of the source of current to the LED (a consumer of current) and fails to engage with the electrochemical mechanism at all.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle may be asked to label the three components of the lemon cell — two electrodes and the liquid — before identifying which is the electrolyte. Students who respond quickly may be asked what would happen if both the copper wire and the nail were made of the same metal.

assessment_items.stage_label: Construct and explain how cells and batteries supply current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can identify the components of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain that a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces electrical current, and evaluate which cell type is more appropriate for a given application with justification.

assessment_items.question_text: A student needs to choose a power source for a TV remote control that is used only occasionally, and a separate source for an electric bicycle that is used every day. Which pairing is most appropriate, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Rechargeable battery for both, because rechargeable batteries are always better than single-use cells.

options.label: B
options.text: Rechargeable battery for the remote and single-use dry cell for the bicycle, because rechargeable batteries are smaller and fit better into remotes.

options.label: C
options.text: Single-use dry cell for both, because dry cells are cheaper to buy and easier to dispose of than rechargeable batteries.

options.label: D
options.text: Single-use dry cell for the remote and rechargeable battery for the bicycle, because the remote's low, infrequent use makes the cost of recharging infrastructure unnecessary, while the bicycle's daily high-energy use makes recharging economical.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals that the student has not considered the trade-offs of rechargeable cells — recharging infrastructure, cost, and wear after multiple cycles — and has applied a simple rule rather than evaluating context.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals that the student is using only immediate cost as the criterion and has not weighed long-term cost, environmental concern, or end-of-life disposal for high-use applications.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals a confusion based on physical size rather than energy and reusability criteria — the student is applying an irrelevant physical attribute to an energy-source decision.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find evaluation tasks difficult may first list two properties of each cell type before attempting the pairing. Students who respond quickly may be asked to identify a third application and justify which cell type suits it.

assessment_items.question_text: A zinc container, a carbon rod with a metal cap, and a moist paste electrolyte are the main parts of a dry cell. Explain the function of each part and state one way the dry cell improves on the Voltaic cell for everyday use.
expected_elements: States that the zinc container is the negative terminal and is one of the two electrodes that takes part in the chemical reaction.
States that the carbon rod with its metal cap is the positive terminal, serving as the second electrode.
States that the moist paste is the electrolyte — it allows the chemical reaction between the electrodes that drives the current.
Identifies at least one improvement over the Voltaic cell — for example, the paste electrolyte makes the cell portable and prevents liquid spillage, unlike the liquid electrolyte of the Voltaic cell.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to describe each part in a sentence may label a blank dry-cell outline diagram with a single-word function for each part before writing. Students who finish quickly may be asked to describe one limitation the dry cell shares with the Voltaic cell despite its improvements.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across magnetic effect, heating effect, and cell operation to explain circuit behaviour
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can produce a causal explanation of how a cell drives current that simultaneously produces a magnetic field in an electromagnet coil and heat in a resistance element, integrating cell chemistry, the magnetic effect, and the heating effect in a single coherent account.

competency.competency_text: Describe how electricity works and demonstrate its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A circuit contains a dry cell, a switch, a nichrome wire, and a coil wound around an iron nail. When the switch is closed, the nichrome wire warms up and the nail attracts iron clips. Which statement correctly explains what is happening inside this circuit at the same moment?

options.label: A
options.text: The cell first powers the nichrome wire, and after it reaches full heat, the remaining energy travels to the coil to create the magnetic field — the two effects happen in sequence.

options.label: B
options.text: The chemical reaction in the cell drives a current simultaneously through both the nichrome wire and the coil; the wire's resistance converts electrical energy to heat while the current in the coil produces a magnetic field around the nail.

options.label: C
options.text: The magnetic field produced by the coil induces the heating in the nichrome wire; without the coil, the wire would not heat up.

options.label: D
options.text: The nichrome wire converts electrical energy to heat, and the heat energy then travels through the connecting wire to the coil where it is converted into a magnetic field.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals that the student treats the two effects as sequential rather than simultaneous — a fundamental misunderstanding of how a single current drives all effects in a circuit at the same time.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reveals a misconception about energy conversion pathways — the student thinks heat from one component is the input for magnetism in another, failing to see that both are direct effects of the same current.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals a reversal of the causal relationship — the student has confused the direction of the electromagnetic induction relationship, applying it in the wrong direction and context.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the integrated circuit scenario difficult may first answer two separate questions — what causes the warming? what causes the magnetic field? — before combining them. Students who respond quickly may be asked what would happen to both effects simultaneously if the cell were replaced with a weaker one.

assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: The student can produce a causal explanation of how a cell drives current that simultaneously produces a magnetic field in an electromagnet coil and heat in a resistance element, integrating cell chemistry, the magnetic effect, and the heating effect in a single coherent account.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'If I use a rechargeable battery instead of a dry cell in my electromagnet circuit, the nail will attract more clips because rechargeable batteries are more powerful.' Evaluate this claim. Is it well-reasoned? What is correct and what is flawed in this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is completely wrong: rechargeable batteries produce alternating current, which cannot power an electromagnet.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is correct but for the wrong reason: rechargeable batteries are stronger because they have more wire turns inside them than dry cells.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is correct: rechargeable batteries always produce more current than dry cells, so the electromagnet will always be stronger.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is partially flawed: the number of clips depends on the current delivered, not the type of cell; if a rechargeable battery and a dry cell deliver the same current, the electromagnet strength will be the same, but a higher-voltage rechargeable battery would indeed increase the current and therefore the strength.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Reveals uncritical acceptance of the student's claim — the respondent has not interrogated what determines current magnitude or electromagnet strength, applying a vague notion that 'rechargeable is more powerful.'
what_each_option_reveals.A: Reveals a misconception about the type of current rechargeable batteries produce — they produce direct current like dry cells; this distractor targets students who confuse rechargeable with mains AC supply.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Reveals the misconception that structural features inside the battery (imagined internal coils) are responsible for electromagnet strength, confusing the circuit's external coil turns with an imagined internal feature.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find evaluation questions difficult may be asked to first identify what the student's argument is actually about — which variable they claim makes the electromagnet stronger — before assessing whether that reasoning is correct. Students who respond quickly may be asked to design a fair test that would resolve the original student's claim.

assessment_items.question_text: A circuit contains a dry cell, a coil of wire wound around an iron nail, a nichrome wire, and a switch. When the switch is closed, two effects are observed at once. Explain, in a connected account, how the dry cell produces current, how that current produces the magnetic effect in the coil, and how the same current produces the heating effect in the nichrome wire. Your explanation should show how all three — cell, magnetic effect, and heating effect — are causally linked in the same circuit.
look_for: Correctly identifies the chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte inside the dry cell as the source of electrical energy that drives the current.
Explains that the current flowing through the coil produces a magnetic field around the nail, making it attract iron objects, and that this field disappears when the current stops.
Explains that the current flowing through the nichrome wire encounters resistance, and that this resistance converts electrical energy into heat energy.
Demonstrates understanding that both effects occur simultaneously in the same circuit because a single current from the cell flows through both components at once.
Uses causal connective language throughout — 'because', 'which causes', 'as a result' — to show that the three phenomena are linked rather than listed.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find the extended writing format challenging may use a numbered sequence of causal steps rather than continuous prose, provided each step names a cause and its effect. Students who complete the task with ease may be asked to extend their account to describe what changes to both the magnetic and heating effects simultaneously if the cell is replaced with one of higher voltage.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Observation when switch is closed | Change made | New observation
A dry cell powers a coil on a nail and a nichrome wire | Nail holds 6 clips; nichrome wire is warm | Second cell added in series | Nail holds 11 clips; nichrome wire is hot
A rechargeable battery powers the same circuit | Nail holds 9 clips; nichrome wire is moderately warm | Number of coil turns doubled | Nail holds 18 clips; nichrome wire remains moderately warm
A lemon Voltaic cell powers a small LED and a thin nichrome wire | LED glows faintly; wire barely warm | Iron nail inserted into coil | LED glows faintly; wire barely warm; nail now holds 2 clips
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. For each scenario: (1) identify which effect — magnetic, heating, or both — changed as a result of the modification; (2) explain why that specific change caused the observed outcome, using the concepts of current, resistance, and magnetic field from this chapter; (3) for Scenario 3, explain why the LED brightness and wire warmth did not change when the nail was inserted, even though the nail now attracts clips.
assessment_items.scaffold: Work through each scenario row by row. For each row: name the effect that changed, state the reason in one or two sentences, and connect your reason to what you know about current, resistance, and magnetic field. For Scenario 3, think carefully about whether inserting the nail into the coil affects the current in the circuit before you explain the LED and nichrome wire observations.
format_of_output: Written responses for each of the three scenarios, addressed row by row

Each scenario response should include: the effect(s) that changed, a causal explanation naming current or resistance or magnetic field, and for Scenario 3 an additional sentence on why LED brightness and wire warmth are unchanged

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires simultaneous causal reasoning across magnetic effect, heating effect, and cell operation in a single circuit; a data table presenting three varied scenarios forces students to apply all three concepts in context rather than recalling any one of them in isolation.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can read experimental data, identify which circuit phenomenon is responsible for each observed change, and construct a causal account that correctly links current magnitude to both magnetic strength and heat production — the full integrated operation named in the dissolution test.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold's row-by-row instruction is deliberate: it prevents students from writing a generic account of all three effects and forces them to engage with each scenario's specific change. Scenario 3 is the diagnostic heart of the task — the insertion of an iron nail strengthens the magnetic field without increasing current, so the heating effect (which depends on current) should be unchanged; a student who correctly identifies this distinction is reasoning at the Analysis–Evaluation level.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses name the specific causal mechanism in each scenario — more cells increase current which simultaneously increases both heat and magnetic strength; more turns increase magnetic strength without changing current so heating is unchanged; inserting an iron nail increases magnetic field concentration without increasing current so the LED and wire are unaffected. Weak responses list observations without explaining why, or attribute all changes to 'more electricity' without distinguishing current from magnetic field or resistance.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the three-scenario structure overwhelming may complete Scenario 1 fully before moving to the others; the teacher may confirm the Scenario 1 response before the student proceeds. Students who complete all three scenarios with ease may be asked to design a fourth scenario row in which both the heating and the magnetic effects increase simultaneously and state what single change would produce it.
